_about: Cross-book name authority for the whole translation shelf. Consult BEFORE romanizing anything in a new book; one rendering per referent ACROSS BOOKS unless a book records a deliberate deviation (e.g. a period-flavor style like Chungking/Peiping in a 1940s memoir) in its own glossary note. Feed every new book's decided renderings back in on completion. Entries carry every rendering observed on the shelf with the books that used it; status 'reconcile' marks a live cross-book disagreement (article-only differences excluded). Sources: the nine completed books, 2026-08.

万国公墓.note: The Shanghai cemetery for the dead of all nations (万国公墓, ‘Cemetery of All Nations’), Chinese and foreign alike, on Hongqiao Road in the western outskirts (founded 1909); Stephen is buried here (ch28–ch29).

三民主义.note: 三民主义; Sun Yat-sen's doctrine of nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood, made the Nationalist creed. See the note at first appearance.

三潭印月.note: A celebrated West Lake scene, an islet ringed by three small stone pagodas standing in the water.

三马路.note: 三马路; the colloquial name of Hankou Road (汉口路), the financial street of Chinese Shanghai where the securities exchange stood. See the footnote at first appearance.

上海.note: China’s largest city and the seat of the Party Central and its underground in this period.

东方饭店.note: The Shanghai hotel (东方, 'the East') where Fourth Madam stages the storytelling that opens A-Chu's origins to him; rendered by pinyin, since the source's 东方饭店 does not map cleanly onto any one attested Republican-era English hotel name.

中原.note: The Central Plains (Zhongyuan) Liberated Area, linked to Chongqing by a secret line Liu Shaowen laid (ch41).

中国民权保障同盟.note: Civil-liberties body founded in Shanghai, December 1932 (Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei, Yang Quan). Chapter 29 (footnoted).

中央特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence/security organ (established 1927-28) that Gu Shunzhang helped run under Zhou Enlai. English 'Central Special Branch' is the form used by Wikipedia (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Special_Branch); 'Special Services Section' and 'Central Department for Special Tasks'

九江.note: 九江; the Yangzi river-port in Jiangxi, below Mount Lu.

于右任.note: 1879–1964; Nationalist elder statesman, calligrapher, and president of the Control Yuan.

云南路.note: 云南路; a Settlement road near the racecourse; older English Yunnan Road.

交际花.note: 交际花, lit. 'a flower of society'; a fashionable woman of the demimonde who moves among wealthy men, here Xu Manli.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, from his code name in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the fake ‘renunciation’ notices and their rebuttal.

兆丰公园.note: 兆丰公园; the large park in the western part of the International Settlement, known in English as Jessfield Park (today Zhongshan Park, 中山公园), with a lake and a small zoo.

先施公司.note: Sincere Co., opened on Nanjing Road, Shanghai, in 1917; one of the 'four great' pre-war department stores. Cited in ch05 as commercial camouflage for moving parcels. Attested in histories of Nanjing Road commerce.

兰心大戏院.note: A Shanghai theatre (the historical Lyceum Theatre); He Yashu says they saw a Shaoxing opera there (Chapter 25). Romanized 'Lanxin' to match the Lanxin Western Restaurant.

关东军.note: The Japanese army in the Northeast; staged the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931. Chapter 28.

内山书店.note: Real. Uchiyama Kanzo's Hongkou bookshop (from 1917; moved 1929 to Scott Road), stocking Japanese and banned left-wing books; Lu Xun's haunt.

军统.note: The Kuomintang's Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (secret police). The name is strictly of 1938; its use for 1931 is a mild anachronism. See the note at Chapter 4.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the ‘Christian General’ and warlord, at this time an anti-Japanese figure.

冯雪峰.note: 1903–1976; poet, literary theorist and CCP cultural figure, liaison to Shanghai’s writers.

北伐.note: Real. The Nationalist-Communist military campaign (1926-28) from Guangzhou to unify China; its approach to Shanghai in 1927 is the backdrop to Cui Wentai's story.

北四川路.note: 北四川路; a main road running north from the Settlement into the Hongkou district; older English North Szechuen Road.

北平.note: The name of Beijing under the Nationalist government (1928–49); site of the Tongyi Company’s largest creditors.

十九路军.note: Real. Cantonese army that fought the Japanese at Shanghai in 1932, later sent against Communists in Fujian.

十人团.note: the 1928 ten-man Liaison Group of Dai Li lore, retrojected to 1927 by the book

华懋饭店.note: Victor Sassoon's Cathay Hotel on the Bund (今和平饭店), the most fashionable hotel of 1930 Shanghai.

南市.note: The old South City district of Shanghai, site of the Nanshi Refugee Zone.

反省院.note: A Nationalist ‘Three People’s Principles’ re-education facility to which unconvicted political prisoners could be transferred, used as a rescue channel.

史良.note: 1900–1985; lawyer, the only woman of the Seven Gentlemen; first Minister of Justice of the PRC.

吴淞口.note: 吴淞口; the mouth of the Huangpu where it meets the Yangtze estuary, the seaward gate of Shanghai; older English Woosung.

吴铁城.note: Kuomintang statesman; former Guangdong governor and later overseas department minister.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976; then the real director of the Party’s underground work in Shanghai; the author’s superior.

唐绍仪.note: 1862-1938; first premier of the Republic, assassinated in Shanghai.

四马路.note: A busy, crowded Shanghai street (present-day Fuzhou Road), rendered by its old foreign-settlement name (Chapter 26).

国民党.note: Rendered ‘Kuomintang’ throughout (not ‘Nationalist Party’); the conventional English name.

国民参政会.note: The wartime advisory body; Dong Biwu and Deng Yingchao launched there a motion against the secret imprisonment of patriots (ch21).

复兴社.note: founded spring 1932; the book has Dai Li organizing its Special Services Section in 1931

外滩.note: 外滩; the riverfront boulevard of the International Settlement (外滩公园, the park on the Bund).

外白渡桥.note: The steel bridge at the mouth of Suzhou Creek, known in the foreign settlements as the Garden Bridge.

大世界.note: The famous many-storeyed amusement palace at the edge of the French Concession (opened 1917); a dance hall behind it is the scene of ch31.

大光明电影院.note: 大光明 ('great brightness'); a famous Shanghai cinema. Here only a passing reference (the girls touting at its door).

大冶.note: County (now city) in Hubei where the author was sent on leaving Qincheng in 1975, her daughter's family being posted there with a geological team (ch40, ch42).

大美晚报.note: Real. The Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, American-owned and foreign-registered; Chinese edition from 16 Jan 1933.

天津.note: North China treaty port; seat of the Party’s Northern Bureau.

委员长.note: For Chiang; 'Chairman' would collide with the CCP usage a reader expects.

孔祥熙.note: H. H. Kung (1881–1967); financier and premier, husband of Song Ailing.

孙传芳.note: Warlord of the five southeastern provinces.

孙科.note: 1891–1973; son of Sun Yat-sen and a president of one of the Nationalist government’s Five Yuan.

孤山.note: An islet-hill in West Lake beside which the Yu Mansion stands.

孤岛.note: The name for the foreign-concession enclave of Shanghai between the Japanese occupation of the surrounding city in 1937 and the seizure of the concessions after Pearl Harbor in December 1941, during which the concessions kept a precarious neutral status.

宋子文.note: Real. Nationalist finance minister 1928-1933; evoked (unnamed) by the hint that 'Mr. Song's' elder brother is a great personage and the bank does Ministry of Finance bond business.

宋美龄.note: 1898–2003; Madame Chiang Kai-shek, youngest of the Soong sisters.

山东.note: 山东; the northern coastal province; older English Shantung.

巡捕房.note: The police stations of the foreign concessions (Shanghai's International Settlement and French Concession). Their Chinese informers were 包打聽.

常州.note: A city in southern Jiangsu on the Shanghai–Nanjing line.

庐山.note: A mountain resort in Jiangxi where Chiang Kai-shek was staying.

廖承志.note: 1908–1983; son of Liao Zhongkai and He Xiangning, CCP leader; arrested in Shanghai in 1933 and among those the author’s circle worked to rescue.

延安.note: The Communist base in northern Shaanxi; Ronghua’s wireless link runs between Shanghai and Yan’an. (The Party’s seat only from 1937; its use in the novel’s earlier setting is a mild anachronism, as with ‘Juntong.’)

张国焘.note: An early CCP leader who, during the Long March, split with the Central Committee over the line of march; later defected to the Kuomintang (1897–1979).

张大千.note: 1899–1983; one of the most celebrated modern Chinese painters.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li / Juntong-affiliated irregular force active in the lower Yangtze during the war; its Hengyang-region commander Zhou Kuilong held the couple (ch21).

愚园路.note: A fashionable road in western Shanghai; the site of Yang Yubo’s mansion.

戈登路.note: International Settlement street, printed in the source in Roman letters too; today Jiangning Road (江宁路).

戴季陶.note: Real (1891-1949). KMT theorist of anti-communism ('Daiism'); reread Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles to exclude the Communists.

戴笠.note: 1897–1946, head of the Nationalists' Military Statistics Bureau (军统/Juntong), the KMT secret service; Whampoa sixth class (did not graduate). Ordered and oversaw the couple's secret arrest (ch20–21).

斧头帮.note: Shanghai assassins' gang; linked to the killing of the China Merchants director.

新华日报.note: The Communist Party’s newspaper in the Nationalist areas.

方志敏.note: 1899–1935; CCP leader of the Northeast Jiangxi soviet; his prison diary was among the papers kept in the Tongyi vault.

旗袍.note: The close-fitting Chinese woman's dress (旗袍, qipao); ‘cheongsam’ is the established English form used throughout.

日本.note: 日本; Japan, named with England as America's two rivals in the East.

暨南大学.note: Overseas-Chinese university in Shanghai where Chen Gaoyong was a professor.

曲江.note: County town in northern Guangdong (present-day Shaoguan); wartime relief hub.

曹锟.note: Real (1862-1938). President of the Republic 1923-24, deposed and placed under arrest in Feng Yuxiang's 1924 coup.

曾家岩.note: The Chongqing district where the Eighth Route Army office (the '八办') stood; site of the narrator's 1942 audience with Zhou Enlai (ch20–21).

望龙门.note: The Chongqing site of the Juntong secret detention house where the narrator was held (ch21).

李公朴.note: 1902–1946; educator, one of the Seven Gentlemen; assassinated at Kunming in 1946.

李国杰.note: Real. Grandson of Li Hongzhang; principal of the 1933 China Merchants embezzlement case, sentenced to eight years.

李宗仁.note: Guangxi Clique leader; later acting president of the Republic of China.

李鸿章.note: 李鸿章 (1823–1901); the late-Qing statesman who launched the self-strengthening state industries Wang Hefu cites as the beginning of Chinese industry.

杜月笙.note: 1888-1951. Foremost of the Shanghai Green Gang 'three tycoons'; first introduced ch06. Pinyin form standard (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du_Yuesheng).

杨杏佛.note: Yang Quan (1893–1933); secretary-general of the China League for the Protection of Civil Rights, assassinated 1933.

杭州.note: Zhejiang provincial capital on West Lake, where the author went into hiding in 1932–33.

枫林桥.note: Landmark on the road out to Longhua.

标金.note: 标金; bar gold of standard fineness traded for future delivery on the Shanghai exchange, the other great speculative market beside the bonds.

梅花山.note: Real. Hill on Purple Mountain, Nanjing, over Sun Quan's tomb; plum-viewing ground planted from 1929. Noted ch26.

歌乐山.note: A hill west of Chongqing; site of Xu Shiying's birthday banquet (ch20).

永安公司.note: Wing On Co., opened on Nanjing Road in 1918 facing Sincere; another of the 'four great' Shanghai department stores. ch05.

法大马路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Jinling East Road; the address on the counter-notice.

法币.note: The Nationalist government's legal-tender paper currency (introduced 1935 in fact; the novel uses the term loosely).

洛阳.note: The ancient capital; in the peony legend Empress Wu Zetian banishes the flower to Luoyang, whence 'the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven' (Chapter 27).

洪门.note: 洪门; the sworn-brotherhood secret society of south China. See the note at 'a Hongmen brother.'

浙江路.note: 浙江路; a Settlement road crossing Nanjing Road; older English Chekiang Road.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu; older English Pootung.

海格路.note: Real. Avenue Haig (after Field Marshal Douglas Haig); today Huashan Road (华山路).

牯岭.note: 牯岭 (also romanized Kuling); the hill-station atop Mount Lu (庐山) above Jiujiang, a summer retreat from the Yangzi heat.

特科.note: The CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service (中央特科), founded 1927 and active in Shanghai; here Yang Muci's and Lao Yu's organ. See the note at Chapter 4.

玄武湖.note: Real. Lake against the northeastern wall of Nanjing.

王新衡.note: A friend of Chiang Ching-kuo and figure in the Military Statistics Bureau.

珞珈山.note: The Wuhan University campus hill where the author met Guo Changlu.

瑞金.note: The seat of the Central Soviet in Jiangxi, capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic.

田汉.note: 1898–1968; playwright and lyricist, author of the words of the PRC national anthem.

申报.note: Shanghai's most famous daily newspaper (1872–1949); among the papers A-Chu lays out for Muci in Chapter 35.

白公馆.note: The household of the Fifth Concubine of the Bai family (白府五姨太), the concubine's sworn sister and protector; also rendered the House of Bai.

白区.note: Kuomintang-controlled territory, as opposed to the Red (soviet) areas; the author’s underground post was in the Shanghai white area.

百乐门.note: The Paramount Ballroom, a famous Shanghai dance hall; here the house to which Young Tang is packed off.

秦邦宪.note: Better known as Bo Gu (博古); one of the ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and de facto Party leader 1931–35.

老闸捕房.note: 老闸捕房; the Louza (老闸) police station of the International Settlement, the very station whose men fired the shots of 30 May 1925.

胡汉民.note: 1879–1936; a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek.

胡蝶.note: 1908–1989, the film star 'Butterfly Wu,' twice voted 'Queen of the Screen'; her lost wartime 'luggage' (largely smuggled goods) and her complaint to Dai Li triggered the couple's arrest (ch20–21).

苏堤.note: 苏堤; the willow-planted dyke across the West Lake, traditionally credited to the poet Su Shi. See the note in Fan Bowen's poem.

英国.note: 英国; Britain, named with Japan as America's two rivals in the East.

蒋经国.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s son; the conventional Wade–Giles English form is used.

虹口.note: 虹口; district of Shanghai north of Suzhou Creek, part of the International Settlement, with many Japanese residents and mills; older English Hongkew.

许广平.note: 1898–1968; educator and writer, wife of Lu Xun; editor of his Complete Works.

谭延闿.note: Hunan military governor and Nationalist elder; first president of the Executive Yuan; signed the Wuhan order expelling Chiang in April 1927.

贺衷寒.note: 1900-1972; Whampoa 1st class, Blue Shirt political-warfare leader

跑马厅.note: 跑马厅 (also 跑马场); the great racecourse of the International Settlement, off Bubbling Well Road (today People’s Square and People’s Park).

钱庄.note: 钱庄; a traditional Chinese private bank or money-shop, distinct from the modern 银行. The silk men's working credit runs through these houses, and it is a native-bank manager who will not stretch a point for Chen Junyi.

长安.note: The Tang capital (modern Xi'an), standing for the far-off imperial city in the tanci aria sung in Chapters 12 and 15.

长江.note: The conventional English form, used throughout.

阎锡山.note: 阎锡山 (1883–1960), the militarist governor of Shanxi (the 'model governor'); in 1930 a leader of the anti-Chiang Northern coalition whose armies drive down the Tianjin–Pukou line in this chapter's war news.

阿英.note: Pen name of Qian Xingcun (1900–1977), writer and literary historian; ran the ‘Wind and Rain Bookroom’ hidden in the Tongyi Company.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944; foreign minister of the Wuhan Nationalist government; conventional English form retained.

陈布雷.note: Chiang Kai-shek’s chief secretary and speechwriter; elder brother of Chen Xunshe.

陈济棠.note: 1890-1954; Guangdong warlord ("the King of the South"), led the 1936 Two Kwangs revolt against Chiang.

陈独秀.note: 1879–1942; first general secretary of the CCP, removed at the August Seventh Conference of 1927.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001; Nationalist organization boss of the ‘CC Clique,’ firmly anti-Communist.

陈赓.note: Whampoa graduate and head of the intelligence (2nd) section of the Party’s Special Branch; later a PLA general.

霞飞路.note: A main thoroughfare of the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Central Huaihai Road.

青岛.note: Shandong port city, host of the Fifth National Bar Association congress (1933).

青木关.note: A place west of Chongqing where the released couple settled 1945 (ch21).

青红帮.note: The Green Gang (青帮) and the Hong/Red Gang (洪帮), the great secret-society brotherhoods of Republican Shanghai; Young Tang names them as A-Chu's likely enemies after the hospital bombing.

静安寺.note: The Jing'an (Bubbling Well) Temple, which gave its name to Bubbling Well Road; the district around it, where the narrator and Helen breakfast (ch29).

静安寺路.note: The concession-era English name of 静安寺路 (today Nanjing West Road, 南京西路).

顾祝同.note: 1893–1987; Kuomintang general, commander of the Third War Zone.

顾顺章.note: Head of the Party’s Special Branch whose 1931 defection to the Kuomintang gravely wrecked the Shanghai underground.

香港.note: British colony; seat of the Party’s Southern Bureau.

马寅初.note: Economist, later famous for advocating population control.

马斯南路.note: Real. Rue Massenet, after the composer Jules Massenet; today Sinan Road (思南路). The recognition-signal address.

鲁迅.note: Pen name of Zhou Shuren (1881-1936); author of The True Story of Ah Q; the central figure of essay 3.

鸡鸣寺.note: Real. Temple by the Nanjing city wall, passed on the drive.

黄包车.note: The man-pulled two-wheeled cab of Republican Shanghai.

黄浦江.note: The river through Shanghai; A-Chu’s men dump the kidnappers’ bodies in it.

黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession patrol house; Chiang Kai-shek was once his disciple.

龙华.note: District in the southern outskirts of Shanghai; site of the Kuomintang Garrison Command’s prison and execution ground.

葛籠重蔵.note: 葛籠 is glossed つづら (Tsuzura) in the text; given name 重蔵 Jūzō. Referred to in narration as 重蔵.

重蔵.note: Bare given name of Tsuzura Jūzō, used throughout the narration.

風間五平.note: 風間 glossed かざま (Kazama); 五平 Gohei.

五平.note: Bare given name of Kazama Gohei.

下柘植次郎左衛門.note: 下柘植 glossed しもつげ (Shimotsuge). In the opening he is 老人, 'the old man'.

次郎左衛門.note: Bare name of Shimotsuge Jirōzaemon in narration; also styled 'the old man' / 'the Master' where the source uses 老人 / お師匠.

木猿.note: Written 木さる in the ch04 title; 木猿 here. Her father wishes she had been a son.

黒阿弥.note: Full form 佐那具ノ黒阿弥, Sanagu-no-Kuroami.

織田信長.note: The warlord whose 1581 invasion destroyed Iga; killed at the Honnō-ji in 1582.

豊臣秀吉.note: Ruler of Japan by 1591; the assassination target of the novel.

家康.note: Tokugawa Ieyasu; crossed Iga in 1582 fleeing the Honnō-ji Incident.

惟任日向守光秀.note: Akechi Mitsuhide, who killed Nobunaga at the Honnō-ji; here under the name and court title Nobunaga had granted him.

丹羽長秀.note: Oda commander on the Yamashiro road in the 1581 invasion; his HQ at Ōyado is the target of the fire-raid.

滝川勝雄.note: Commander of Maruyama Castle in the novel; reading of 勝雄 not independently confirmed.

信雄.note: Oda Nobunaga's son, adopted into the Kitabatake house of Ise; led the failed first Iga campaign.

柘植清広.note: Also 柘植太郎清広. Named leader of the Iga league in the novel.

百地新之丞.note: An Iga gōshi of Tatsunokuchi, of the Momochi band.

楯岡ノ道順.note: Legendary Iga jōnin (a.k.a. Momochi Sandayū); commander of the hundred-man shinobi corps.

葛籠太郎兵衛.note: Jūzō's ailing father, killed in the invasion.

今井宗久.note: Sakai merchant and tea master high in Hideyoshi's favor; the secret paymaster of the plot.

千宗易.note: Sen no Rikyū, the great tea master; here under his lay name Sōeki.

音羽ノ城戸.note: Iga genin; historically the marksman who ambushed Nobunaga at the Aekuni Shrine.

松永久秀/弾正久秀/久秀.note: The warlord who burned the Tōdai-ji Great Buddha in 1567; 弾正 (Danjō) is his court title. Died 1577.

松倉蔵人/蔵人.note: The scarred leader in the Aizen-dō, who claims to be a rōnin of the Shibata house; Jūzō takes him for a broken Mino bandit and kills him. 蔵人 doubles as a court-office name, hence Jūzō's mockery.

雲兵衛.note: The young ex-sailor and one-time balladeer in Matsukura's band; Jūzō spares and conscripts him.

懸巣ノ次郎.note: Matsukura's foster-retainer, found stabbed dead beneath the Great Buddha. 懸巣 = a jay.

小萩.note: The taciturn Nara courtesan who is in fact Imai Sōkyū's guide-agent, sent to meet Jūzō; a Kōga woman, Jūzō suspects.

武田勝頼.note: Last lord of the Takeda of Kai; destroyed by Nobunaga and Ieyasu in 1582.

伊勢屋嘉兵衛.note: The Kyōto shopkeeper's cover identity Jūzō assigns to Kuroami at the end of ch01.

三好三人衆.note: The three Miyoshi captains who contested control of the Kinai after 1564; Matsunaga's war with them burned the Great Buddha.

今井宗薫.note: Son of Imai Sōkyū; formal name Tatewaki Saemon. A tea master and merchant in his own right.

宗薫.note: Bare given name of Imai Sōkun.

惣五郎.note: The Sakai loafer (遊び人) from the Daimoku Hall who guides Jūzō to the pleasure quarter; a minor invented character.

会田源右衛門.note: The false name Jūzō gives in Sakai, posing as a gōshi of Kanbara in Echigo.

武野紹鴎.note: 1502–1555; Sakai tea master who shaped the wabi style and taught both Sōkyū and Rikyū.

納屋宗次.note: Sakai merchant and tea man whose son-in-law and heir Sōkyū became.

今井信経.note: Sōkyū's claimed grandfather, said to have been lord of Imaichi Castle in Ōmi.

出羽守宗慶.note: Sōkyū's claimed father, who drifted from Ōmi into Yamato.

足利義昭.note: The fifteenth and last Ashikaga shogun, installed by Nobunaga in 1568.

藤吉郎.note: The early name of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, when he was a lieutenant of Nobunaga.

浅井長政.note: Lord of Odani Castle in Ōmi and Nobunaga's brother-in-law, turned enemy; besieged from 1570.

小西隆佐.note: Sakai merchant risen from a face-powder shop, favored by Hideyoshi as Sōkyū's rival; father of Konishi Yukinaga.

小西行長.note: Ryūsa's son, made Settsu-no-kami and a daimyō; a great Christian lord, executed after Sekigahara.

行長.note: Bare name of Konishi Yukinaga (given as Yakurō Yukinaga / Settsu-no-kami Yukinaga).

秀次.note: Hideyoshi's nephew and adopted heir, made Kampaku in 1591; forced to suicide in 1595.

千利休.note: The supreme tea master; the same man recorded elsewhere under his lay name 千宗易 Sen no Sōeki.

前田玄以.note: Hideyoshi's magistrate of Kyoto (Kyoto shoshidai/bugyō), a former monk who administered the capital and its temples; Gohei's new master, at 200 koku.

前田.note: The Maeda house of Maeda Gen'i (distinct from the Kaga Maeda).

加藤肥後守.note: Katō Kiyomasa, under his court title Governor of Higo; the Iga man Kuranawate-no-Shishiji was killed for entering his service.

以天仰山.note: The eccentric monk-abbot of the Chinnō-in who buries himself in the bamboo grove; a fictional figure. Reading of 以天 not independently confirmed.

仰山.note: Bare name of the abbot Iten Gyōzan.

蔵縄手ノ鹿次.note: An Iga man cut down by his own comrades in the spring of 1591 for taking service with Katō Kiyomasa; reading of 鹿次 (Shishiji) not independently confirmed.

下呂正兵衛康次.note: The false name Gohei adopts after deserting Iga, claiming descent from a retainer surname of the old Ichijō house of Tosa. Furigana げろ on 下呂; reading of 康次 (Yasuji) a project call.

服部半蔵.note: The historical Iga ninja who served Tokugawa Ieyasu; here recalled by Jūzō as the broker between the Tokugawa and the Iga gōshi. Footnoted at first appearance.

石見守.note: The honorary provincial title Hattori Hanzō later took (Governor of Iwami).

光秀.note: Akechi Mitsuhide, Nobunaga's killer at Honnō-ji, defeated by Hideyoshi at Yamazaki. Bare surname-reading used in ch05 narration; see 明智光秀.

勝家.note: Shibata Katsuie, Nobunaga's senior general, passed over by Hideyoshi after Yamazaki. Bare given name; see 柴田勝家.

夏見ノ耳次.note: A masterless Iga rappa Kuroami singles out at the muster. 夏見 (Natsumi) is a place in Iga; reading of 耳次 (Mimiji) unglossed in the scan and a project call.

渡辺慧.note: The Kashima-school rōnin swordsman whom Kohagi bankrolls and sets against Jūzō; a fictional figure. The given name 慧 is left unglossed in the scan; the reading Satoru is a project call. Referred to in narration by the bare given name 慧.

榊原康政.note: One of Tokugawa Ieyasu's 'Four Guardians'; here the lieutenant whose letter of introduction sends Watanabe to Imai Sōkyū. Bare 康政 (Yasumasa) also used in narration.

塚原卜伝.note: 1489–1571; the great swordsman of the Kashima tradition, sword-teacher to the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru. Bare 卜伝 (Bokuden) also used.

松林左馬助.note: The Kashima shrine-family swordsman credited with codifying the Kashima-ryū (a.k.a. Shinmei-ryū). Reading of the name not independently confirmed.

足利義輝.note: The thirteenth Ashikaga shogun (r. 1546–1565), a noted swordsman who studied under Bokuden; distinct from Yoshiaki, the last shogun.

宮本武蔵.note: 1584?–1645; the celebrated swordsman and author of the Book of Five Rings, whose duel with the Yoshioka school of Kyoto is legendary. Named here in a proleptic aside ('the later Musashi').

平重盛.note: 1138–1179; eldest son of Taira no Kiyomori, whose mansion once stood at Komatsudani (hence his sobriquet, the Komatsu Minister).

義仲.note: Minamoto (Kiso) no Yoshinaka, 1154–1184; the rough eastern warrior-cousin of Yoshitsune, briefly master of the capital before his fellow Minamoto destroyed him.

妙兵衛.note: One of the rappa in Kohagi's employ, disguised as a timid shop-clerk; guides Watanabe to the ambush.

すね次.note: Another of Kohagi's rappa, posted in the streets around the Jurakudai. Reading a project call (すね次, unglossed).

長曾我部.note: The Chōsokabe house of Tosa; here the Kyoto mansion (of 長曾我部宮内少輔, Chōsokabe Kunai-no-shōyū) whose back wall Jūzō vaults during the ambush.

弥九郎.note: The childhood/common name of 小西行長 Konishi Yukinaga, kept in use by the Sakai merchants who had known him from boyhood; here in Kumobei's gossip.

毛利.note: The great western house of Mōri; one of the daimyō rumored to be behind the Jurakudai fire.

細川.note: The Hosokawa house; another named in the same street rumor.

徳川.note: The Tokugawa house (Ieyasu's); named among the rumored authors of the fire.

宣祖.note: 宣祖 (Korean Sŏnjo, Japanese reading Senso), the reigning king of Chosŏn Korea (r. 1567–1608). The rumor that Yakurō was in league with his 'mother Hei' is Shiba's own baseless street-talk; footnoted.

石田三成.note: Ishida Mitsunari (1560-1600), Hideyoshi’s ablest administrator and one of the Five Commissioners; led the western coalition against Ieyasu and was defeated at Sekigahara. Appears here by his court title Jibu-no-shōyū.

清正.note: Katō Kiyomasa; here by his title Higo-no-kami. Footnoted at first appearance in ch04.

正則.note: Fukushima Masanori, a smith’s son raised by Hideyoshi; named here only as a foil for Gen’i’s obscure birth.

前川十郎左衛門.note: A squad-leader (kumigashira) of the Kyoto magistracy, Gohei’s immediate superior.

藤本安兵衛.note: A squad-leader of the Kyoto magistracy whose men gave chase at Yanagimachi.

金森.note: Kanamori Hida-no-kami Yoshishige (1558-1615), a tea-connoisseur daimyō; the collector whose mansion Gohei raids.

春蟬.note: A courtesan of Yanagimachi; the informer Jūzō kills. Furigana はるぜみ.

信忠.note: Oda Nobutada, Nobunaga’s heir, who took his own life at Nijō castle during the Honnō-ji revolt.

三法師.note: Nobunaga’s infant grandson and legitimate heir, later Oda Hidenobu (Chūnagon of Gifu); Gen’i was charged to protect him.

摩利洞玄.note: The old Kōga master Gen'i owes his life to; born Ban Tōnai (伴藤内) of the Ban house, retired as 洞玄 Dōgen. Bears the Kōga byname 摩利/摩利支天 (Marishiten); called 甲賀ノ摩利 'Mari of Kōga'.

洞玄.note: Bare name of Mari Dōgen, used throughout the narration.

望月刑部左衛門.note: Gyōbuzaemon Shigehisa (重久) of the Mochizuki house of Kōga; raised Kohagi and taught her the Kōga arts; died at Ishida Mitsunari's Kyoto mansion.

刑部左衛門.note: Bare name of Mochizuki Gyōbuzaemon in dialogue.

抜関斎.note: Buddhist name of Sasaki (Rokkaku) Yoshikata (六角義賢), last lord of the Sasaki of Ōmi; Kohagi's true father. Later took the further name 承禎入道 Jōtei.

承禎入道.note: Later Buddhist name of Yoshikata / Hakkansai after his fall and tonsure in Kōga.

淀君.note: Hideyoshi's favored concubine (Yodo-dono), daughter of Azai Nagamasa and niece of Nobunaga; mother of Tsurumatsu and, in 1593, of Hideyori.

秀頼.note: Toyotomi Hideyori, Hideyoshi's son and heir, born to Yodo-gimi on the third day of the eighth month, Bunroku 2 (1593); infant name O-Hiroi.

利家.note: Maeda Toshiie, one of Hideyoshi's most senior generals and a boyhood comrade.

名張ノ耳.note: 名張ノ耳; 耳 (Mimi, 'ear') is a by-name from his keen hearing. A former Iga ninja of the Tsuge faction turned beggar, then Kōga informer; footnoted at first appearance in ch13.

島左近.note: Shima Sakon (Kiyooki, also read Katsutake; d. 1600), a famed warrior whom Ishida Mitsunari coaxed out of retirement by giving him nearly half his own stipend to serve as chief retainer. He commanded the Ishida vanguard and fell at Sekigahara in 1600. In this chapter he governs the Fushimi mansion in Mitsunari's absence.

左近.note: Bare name of Shima Sakon, used throughout the narration and dialogue.

勝猛.note: Given name of Shima Sakon; he refers to himself by it.

伊賀.note: The 'hidden country', home province of the ninja.

甲賀.note: The neighboring ninja district in Ōmi.

御斎峠.note: 御斎峠 (usually Otodo-tōge) is glossed おとぎとうげ in the text, matching the chapter title おとぎ峠; site of Jūzō's grandfather's hermitage.

大屋戸.note: Crossroads hamlet north of Kashiwara; Niwa Nagahide's HQ in 1581.

柏原.note: Site of the Iga gōshi's last-stand fort in 1581.

堺.note: The merchant port; home of Imai Sōkyū.

敢国神社.note: The ichinomiya (first shrine) of Iga province.

東大寺.note: The great Nara temple; its colossal bronze Vairocana is the 'rain-soaked Buddha' of the chapter.

二月堂.note: The Hall of the Second Month at Tōdai-ji.

油坂.note: A slope on the eastern edge of Nara where Jūzō takes an inn.

飛火野.note: A meadow in the Kasuga precinct of Nara.

駿河.note: Coastal province east of Kai; on the Tōkaidō.

呂宋.note: The northern Philippines, newly under Spanish rule from Manila.

愛染堂.note: A hall of Aizen Myō-ō in the ruined Tōdai-ji cloister; the scene of the killing.

多聞院.note: A cloister of Kōfuku-ji whose diary, the Tamon-in nikki, records the 1567 fire.

大坂.note: Site of Hideyoshi's great castle from 1583; the port to which Sakai's trade was drawn off.

芥川.note: In the Nishinari district of Settsu; site of Nobunaga's field camp on his 1568 march to Kyoto.

茨木.note: Town in Settsu, north-east of Ōsaka.

小谷城.note: Azai Nagamasa's stronghold in northern Ōmi.

山崎.note: In Yamashiro, between Kyoto and Ōsaka; where Hideyoshi defeated Akechi Mitsuhide in 1582.

大徳寺.note: The great Rinzai Zen monastery in Murasakino, north Kyoto, closely tied to the tea masters; site of Nobunaga's funeral.

関ヶ原.note: The 1600 battle that founded the Tokugawa shogunate.

塩飽.note: Island group in the Inland Sea, home of noted seafarers.

小豆島.note: Large island in the Inland Sea.

九州.note: The southern main island; Hideyoshi's campaign to subdue it fell in 1587.

越後.note: Province on the Japan Sea coast; the far-off country of Jūzō's assumed identity.

泉州.note: Izumi province (Senshū), in which Sakai lay.

我孫子村.note: Village on the outskirts of Sakai, Sōkyū's fief and foundry settlement.

白毫寺.note: A temple on a hill at the eastern edge of Nara.

四条.note: The Fourth Avenue of Kyoto (and its riverbank, 四条の河原, and bridge, 四条大橋, over the Kamo).

三条.note: The Third Avenue of Kyoto; the site of Gohei's official residence.

鴨川.note: The river running north to south through the capital.

如意ヶ岳.note: A low mountain in the Higashiyama range east of Kyoto, later famous for the 大文字 bonfire; its western slope is Daimonji-yama.

青蓮院.note: A monzeki (imperial-abbot) temple at the northern foot of Higashiyama.

祇園.note: The district below the Yasaka Shrine; not yet a quarter of teahouses in 1591, as the narration notes.

建仁寺.note: The great Rinzai Zen monastery east of the Kamo, at the foot of Higashiyama.

松原通.note: An east-west street of the capital, running toward Kiyomizu.

六波羅.note: A district on the east bank of the Kamo below Higashiyama, once the seat of the Taira and of the Kamakura shogunate's Kyoto office.

清水.note: Kiyomizu-dera, the great temple on the Higashiyama slope; its pagoda is the landmark seen from the fields.

珍皇院.note: A half-ruined, landless temple in the Rokuhara district where the monk Gyōzan lodges travelers; evokes the real Rokudō-Chinnō-ji. Reading a project call.

土佐.note: The province on the south of Shikoku; the old Ichijō house whose retainer-surname Gohei borrows had ruled part of it.

羅刹谷.note: The chapter-title valley south of Higashiyama, its ruined Yakushi hall the rappa's muster-place. 羅刹 (rakshasa) footnoted at first appearance.

泉山.note: The maple-covered peak south of Higashiyama on which the Sennyū-ji stands; read Senzan (the mountain of 泉涌寺).

泉涌寺.note: The imperial mortuary temple on Senzan. Footnoted at first appearance.

音無川.note: The thin stream running through Rakshasa Valley to the Kamo; furigana おとなしがわ. The name means 'the soundless river'.

浮世橋.note: The vermilion bridge into the valley; furigana うきよばし. Named for the 'floating world'; to cross it is to leave the world of the living.

下京.note: The southern, mercantile half of Kyoto.

方広寺.note: Hideyoshi's Great Buddha temple in the capital; Kuroami's whetter-stall stands beside it. The Great Buddha itself was footnoted in ch03.

佐渡.note: The island whose gold mines Hideyoshi engrossed.

生野.note: The silver-mining district in Tajima; furigana いくの.

聚楽第.note: Hideyoshi's palace-villa in the capital (ch07's title, 聚楽). Footnoted at first appearance.

江戸.note: Ieyasu's eastern seat, the future Tokugawa capital; here in a proleptic aside about Hattori Hanzō's later mansion.

関東.note: The eastern provinces, Ieyasu's domain of 2,550,000 koku.

朝鮮.note: Target of Hideyoshi's invasion; the campaign was footnoted in ch03.

大明.note: Ming China, the ultimate object of Hideyoshi's continental war.

四国.note: One of the regions levied for corvée labor for the invasion.

中国.note: The western provinces of the main island (NOT China); rendered 'the Chūgoku provinces' to avoid confusion with 大明.

五畿内.note: The five provinces around the capital (Yamashiro, Yamato, Kawachi, Izumi, Settsu).

二条.note: The Second Avenue of Kyoto; here its eastern edge and the Nijō riverbank (二条河原) by the Kamo, where Kohagi meets Gohei.

阿弥陀ヶ峰.note: A peak of the Higashiyama range south-east of the capital; Hideyoshi would later be entombed on it.

小松谷.note: A wooded hollow at the eastern foot of Amidagamine, named from Taira no Shigemori's old mansion; site of Sōkyū's Kyoto villa, where Kohagi lives.

常陸.note: An eastern province (modern Ibaraki), seat of the Kashima Shrine and the Kashima sword tradition.

鹿島.note: The great shrine of Hitachi and the sword tradition that grew from its shrine-families; paired with Katori as the twin fountainheads of Japanese swordsmanship.

香取.note: The great shrine of Shimōsa, across the river from Kashima; the other cradle of the classical sword schools.

坂東.note: The old name for the eastern provinces (the Kantō), 'east of the passes'.

大坂城.note: Hideyoshi's great stronghold, to which he had removed from the Jurakudai, leaving the Kyoto palace lightly guarded.

柳町.note: The licensed pleasure quarter of the capital in this period, in Nakagyō.

若狭屋.note: The Yanagimachi brothel where Watanabe keeps a favorite; a minor invented setting.

中京.note: The central district of Kyoto, between the upper and lower city.

近衛.note: The premier regent-house of the court nobility; here its Kyoto mansion, a landmark on the skyline.

丸太町.note: An east–west street of the capital, north of the Jurakudai.

堺町.note: A street/quarter of the capital (not the port city of Sakai); one of the crossings watched by Kohagi's rappa.

内野.note: The Uchino, the open ground in the northwest of the capital (the old palace site) on which Hideyoshi raised the Jurakudai.

大宮.note: A north–south avenue of the capital; the eastern bound of the Jurakudai.

浄福寺.note: A temple giving its name to the street that bounded the Jurakudai on the west.

下長者町.note: A street bounding the Jurakudai on the south; Jūzō approaches by its eastern corner.

天竺.note: Tenjiku, the old Japanese name for India — shorthand for the farthest edge of the known world; footnoted.

宇土.note: Uto, in Higo (modern Kumamoto), Konishi Yukinaga's castle-town and fief.

粟田.note: Awata(guchi), the district at the eastern approach to the capital below Higashiyama; a scholar's academy there is the model for Kohagi's villa.

高麗.note: 高麗 (Kōrai/Koryŏ), an older name for Korea; used in Jūzō's aside. The standard rendering for 朝鮮 elsewhere is also Korea.

蓬莱.note: Hōrai (Chinese Penglai), the mythic island-mountain of the immortals; here evoked by the tower's shape. Footnoted.

真葛ヶ原.note: A moor at the western foot of Higashiyama, east of the capital, famed in poetry for its autumn bush-clover.

釜山城.note: Pusan (Busan), the first Korean fortress taken in the 1592 invasion. Added so the entry does not collide with 山城 (Yamashiro) as a substring.

吉野.note: Mountainous district south of Nara, celebrated since antiquity for its cherry blossoms; the setting of Hideyoshi's 1594 flower-viewing progress.

乱波.note: A Kantō term for a shinobi/spy; used interchangeably with 忍び in the text.

伊賀ノ乱.note: The Tenshō Iga War; Nobunaga's 1581 invasion (Tenshō 9).

当薬.note: The dried herb Swertia japonica, a bitter folk stomach remedy.

愛染明王.note: The 'wisdom king' of passion, Rāgarāja; a patron of love.

毘廬遮那仏.note: The cosmic Buddha; the Tōdai-ji colossus is a Vairocana.

法印.note: “Seal of the Law”, the highest Buddhist priestly rank, also conferred by the court on distinguished laymen.

法眼.note: “Eye of the Law”, the rank below Hōin, likewise granted to laymen of note.

大蔵卿.note: Titular Minister of the Treasury; Sōkyū's honorary court office.

関白.note: Imperial Regent, Hideyoshi's supreme office of state from 1585.

松島肩衝.note: A celebrated shouldered tea-caddy; Sōkyū's gift of it to Nobunaga made his fortune.

天下布武.note: “Cover the realm in arms”, Nobunaga's seal motto from 1567.

南蛮.note: “Southern Barbarian”: the Japanese term for Europeans and their goods.

斤.note: A unit of weight, about 600 grams (a catty).

摂津守.note: “Governor of Settsu”, a court title; borne here by Konishi Yukinaga.

北政所.note: Title of the principal wife of a Regent; here Hideyoshi's wife.

竹ノ上人.note: The local nickname for the monk Gyōzan, who gazes at (and claims to become) the bamboo. 上人 (Shōnin) is an honorific for a holy monk.

羅刹.note: A flesh-eating demon of Buddhist myth. Footnoted at first appearance.

国広.note: Horikawa Kunihiro, a celebrated swordsmith; here the maker of the blade Jūzō leaves to be polished.

庚申.note: The kōshin folk-cult and its emblematic monkey; the 'kōshin monkey' simile is footnoted at first appearance.

くノ一.note: The ninja's cant word for a female agent, from breaking the character 女 (woman) into the strokes ku-no-ichi (く-ノ-一). Footnoted at first appearance.

忍び文字.note: 'Shinobi writing': the secret syllabic script ninja used among themselves. The chapter title; footnoted where the device is explained.

吉祥天女.note: The Buddhist goddess of beauty and good fortune (Sanskrit Lakṣmī / Śrī); a byword for a lovely face. Footnoted at first appearance.

革水蜘蛛.note: A ninja flotation device (mizugumo, 'water-spider'): a deerskin float that turns the wearer into a one-man raft. The fiction's own furniture; described in the text.

忍び熊手.note: A collapsible climbing-rake of jointed bamboo on a hemp cord that stiffens into a pole; a ninja tool, described in the text.

七方出.note: The shinobi art of transforming into seven social types (monk, yamabushi, komūsō, mendicant conjuror, sarugaku player, merchant, ordinary man). Self-explained in the text.

摩利支天.note: Marīcī, the deva of the heat-shimmer; guardian deity of warriors and of the Iga/Kōga ninja. The Kōga byname of surpassing adepts.

甲賀三郎.note: Legendary founding ancestor of Kōga ninjutsu, hero of the medieval 甲賀三郎 tale.

甲賀文.note: Fictional Kōga calling-card: a single Sanskrit glyph on a slip, left as a ninja's greeting-token when entering another's territory.
